questions.stem: In RSA, what are the formulas for encryption and decryption?
questions.hint: Check key-generation conditions as well as modular arithmetic.

answer.text: Textbook RSA encrypts c=m^e mod n and decrypts m=c^d mod n, for 0≤m<n. Here n=pq, e is coprime to φ=(p−1)(q−1), and d=e^−1 mod φ. Real RSA additionally requires appropriate standardized padding.
answer.explanation: SEC19 supplies the formulas and their key-generation preconditions. The modular-inverse condition is necessary for a valid key pair, so arbitrary e values are not acceptable. These arithmetic expressions teach RSA operations; raw unpadded modular exponentiation is not a complete secure deployment recipe.

evidence.quote: For textbook RSA choose distinct primes p,q; n=pq and φ=(p-1)(q-1). Choose 1<e<φ with gcd(e,φ)=1, then compute d=e^-1 modφ. Public key is (n,e), private includes d. Encrypt 0≤m<n by c=m^e modn; decrypt by m=c^d modn. Use modular repeated squaring for large exponents. Real RSA requires appropriate standardized padding; raw arithmetic is not a secure deployment recipe.
With p=3,q=13,e=3,m=5, 5^3 mod39=8 arithmetically, but gcd(3,24)=3, so e has no inverse and this is not a valid RSA key.
Check key validity before treating arithmetic results as a working encryption/decryption pair.

questions.stem: In textbook RSA key generation with p=7, q=19 and φ=108, choose the smallest integer e greater than 1 satisfying 1<e<φ and gcd(e,φ)=1. What is e?
questions.hint: Check key-generation conditions as well as modular arithmetic.

answer.explanation: The exponent must be greater than one, below 108 and coprime to 108. Testing candidates in increasing order, 2 shares factor 2, 3 shares factor 3 and 4 shares factor 2 with 108. Five shares neither prime factor of 108, so gcd(5,108)=1. It is therefore the smallest admissible exponent. Other values can also be admissible, but the explicit smallest-value rule makes this open-ended answer unique.

evidence.quote: For textbook RSA choose distinct primes p,q; n=pq and φ=(p-1)(q-1). Choose 1<e<φ with gcd(e,φ)=1, then compute d=e^-1 modφ. Public key is (n,e), private includes d. Encrypt 0≤m<n by c=m^e modn; decrypt by m=c^d modn. Use modular repeated squaring for large exponents. Real RSA requires appropriate standardized padding; raw arithmetic is not a secure deployment recipe.
With p=7,q=19, n=133 and φ=108, e=5 is the smallest admissible e>1, but 7 and other coprime choices also work.
With p=3,q=13,e=3,m=5, 5^3 mod39=8 arithmetically, but gcd(3,24)=3, so e has no inverse and this is not a valid RSA key.

questions.stem: What is the Playfair cipher and what unique element does its grid contain?
questions.hint: Identify the cipher's unit, key structure and assumptions before judging its strength.

answer.text: Playfair is a digraph substitution cipher using a keyed 5×5 letter grid, commonly combining I and J into one cell. It encrypts pairs by same-row, same-column or rectangle rules; fillers and padding must be specified.
answer.explanation: SEC14 explains the 25-cell grid and letter-pair operations. Combining I/J is the conventional element that fits the alphabet into the grid, not a claim about numeric cells. Repeated-letter fillers and final padding affect actual ciphertext, so computations require those conventions rather than guessing them.

evidence.quote: Playfair uses a keyed 5×5 grid, commonly combining I/J, and encrypts letter pairs. Specify duplicate-letter fillers and padding. Same row moves right, same column moves down, and rectangle pairs take the other column in their original row; decryption reverses shifts.

questions.stem: What is ARP Spoofing and which OSI layer does it target?
questions.hint: Identify the trust claim or communication mapping being abused.

answer.text: ARP spoofing supplies false local IPv4-to-MAC associations, directing traffic toward an unintended link endpoint. It targets local link-address resolution at the network/data-link boundary and is commonly treated as a data-link-layer attack.
answer.explanation: SEC05 identifies the poisoned association rather than DNS names or transport state. Its scope is local IPv4-to-MAC resolution, so describing it simply as arbitrary IP routing would miss the mechanism. The layer answer refers to manipulating the local link mapping, while ARP connects network and link addressing.

evidence.quote: Masquerade claims another identity. ARP spoofing poisons local IPv4-to-MAC associations; DNS spoofing/cache poisoning supplies false name resolutions; IP spoofing falsifies a source address. An intermediary attack intercepts and can alter exchanges. A replay reuses a valid old message; nonces, timestamps and sequence checks can reject it. Session hijacking steals or predicts a valid session token. Protect transport, regenerate session IDs after login, restrict cookies and check authorization server-side on every sensitive request.

questions.stem: What three primary services does IPSec provide?
questions.hint: Match the communication task to the protocol and trace key handling separately from signing.

answer.text: The principal IPsec services are confidentiality, integrity and origin authentication for IP traffic. They depend on the chosen protocol/association: AH supplies integrity/authentication without encryption, while ESP can supply confidentiality and integrity; IKE negotiates associations and keys.
answer.explanation: IPsec operates at the network layer, with distinct AH, ESP and IKE roles. Listing the service set must not imply every IPsec packet is encrypted or that IKE itself carries protected application content. Transport/tunnel mode describes coverage/encapsulation rather than replacing the service-selection and key assumptions.

evidence.quote: SSH protects remote login, commands and file transfer such as SFTP; it supports host keys and several client-authentication methods. IPsec protects IP traffic at network layer. AH provides integrity/origin authentication, not encryption; ESP can provide confidentiality and integrity; IKE negotiates security associations and keys. Transport mode protects upper-layer payload; tunnel mode encapsulates an inner IP packet inside an outer header. A VPN is a logical private connection; its actual security depends on the chosen authenticated tunnel.

questions.stem: How does a TCP SYN flood attack work?
questions.hint: Match the resource bottleneck or wireless mechanism to the relevant protection layer.

answer.text: A TCP SYN flood creates many incomplete connection handshakes, occupying server state and exhausting resources needed for legitimate connections. Rate limits, SYN cookies, filtering or upstream controls address different parts of that resource bottleneck.
answer.explanation: SEC06 defines the attack by incomplete-handshake state consumption. The goal is denial of usable service, not necessarily gaining control of the target. Defenses must match the constrained resource and traffic path; no single listed measure guarantees resistance to every distributed load or bandwidth bottleneck.

evidence.quote: DoS exhausts or disables a resource; distributed DoS uses multiple sources, often bots or reflected/amplified responses. A SYN flood leaves many incomplete TCP handshakes occupying state. DNS flooding targets query capacity; NXDOMAIN attacks generate queries for nonexistent names to stress resolvers. Fragment floods abuse reassembly or packet-processing resources. Rate limits, SYN cookies, filtering and upstream capacity controls address different bottlenecks.
Passive attacks observe without changing the target exchange: sniffing and traffic analysis.
Rogue access points imitate or bypass approved wireless service.

questions.stem: What is the difference between SSL and TLS?
questions.hint: Distinguish peer identity, channel protection and risks outside that channel.

answer.text: TLS is the successor to obsolete SSL and provides an authenticated protected channel. Handshakes negotiate parameters, authenticate peers as required and establish keys; symmetric authenticated record protection carries data. Exact handshake messages depend on TLS version.
answer.explanation: SEC21 warns against treating an old SSL/ChangeCipherSpec narrative as the universal TLS1.3 sequence. The useful distinction is protocol succession and version-specific behavior, not a claim that the names are interchangeable or that every deployment of either is automatically secure.

evidence.quote: A certificate binds a public key to a named subject through an issuer signature. Validate the chain to a trusted root, intended hostname, time validity and applicable key usage/revocation policy. A genuine certificate is not proof that a business is honest.
Exact messages depend on TLS version: the old ChangeCipherSpec narrative is not a universal TLS1.3 sequence.
TLS succeeds obsolete SSL and supplies an authenticated protected channel.

questions.stem: What does HTTPS stand for and what security does it add over HTTP?
questions.hint: Distinguish peer identity, channel protection and risks outside that channel.

answer.text: HTTPS is secure HTTP: HTTP over TLS. It adds authenticated channel protection for HTTP paths, headers and content. It does not conceal all metadata, such as endpoint IPs/timing, or protect plaintext after a compromised endpoint decrypts it.
answer.explanation: SEC21 identifies the composition and coverage. Protection depends on authentication and certificate validation rather than the mere appearance of the URL scheme. It concerns the communication channel; endpoint compromise and visible traffic metadata remain outside that confidentiality boundary.

evidence.quote: A certificate binds a public key to a named subject through an issuer signature. Validate the chain to a trusted root, intended hostname, time validity and applicable key usage/revocation policy. A genuine certificate is not proof that a business is honest.
It protects HTTP paths, headers and content on the channel, but does not hide all metadata such as IP endpoints and traffic timing, nor protect data after a compromised endpoint decrypts it.
HTTPS is HTTP over TLS.

questions.stem: What is DNS Spoofing?
questions.hint: Identify the trust claim or communication mapping being abused.

answer.text: DNS spoofing provides false name-resolution data, potentially redirecting a requested domain to an attacker-chosen destination. Cache poisoning is a form that places false answers in a resolver cache. DNSSEC authenticates DNS data when appropriately deployed and validated.
answer.explanation: SEC05 distinguishes false DNS mapping from ARP/IP spoofing. SEC06 separates DNS flooding, which consumes query capacity, from answer authenticity. A successful-looking name lookup can still be maliciously wrong; checking that a response exists is different from establishing its trusted origin and integrity.

evidence.quote: Masquerade claims another identity. ARP spoofing poisons local IPv4-to-MAC associations; DNS spoofing/cache poisoning supplies false name resolutions; IP spoofing falsifies a source address. An intermediary attack intercepts and can alter exchanges. A replay reuses a valid old message; nonces, timestamps and sequence checks can reject it. Session hijacking steals or predicts a valid session token. Protect transport, regenerate session IDs after login, restrict cookies and check authorization server-side on every sensitive request.
DNS flooding targets query capacity; NXDOMAIN attacks generate queries for nonexistent names to stress resolvers.

Match a defense to its layer: authenticated IPsec can resist IP impersonation, DNSSEC authenticates DNS data, TLS authenticates/protects application transport, and bounds-safe code prevents overflows.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of SSH (Secure Shell)?
questions.hint: Match the communication task to the protocol and trace key handling separately from signing.

answer.text: SSH (Secure Shell) protects remote login, command execution and file transfer such as SFTP. It uses host keys and supports several client-authentication methods. Correct host-key validation and restricted management access remain important.
answer.explanation: SEC22 states the protected remote-administration functions. SSH is not merely encryption of a password; it protects the session and requires authentic peer identity. File transfer through SFTP is related to SSH rather than being ordinary FTP with a new name.

evidence.quote: SSH protects remote login, commands and file transfer such as SFTP; it supports host keys and several client-authentication methods. IPsec protects IP traffic at network layer. AH provides integrity/origin authentication, not encryption; ESP can provide confidentiality and integrity; IKE negotiates security associations and keys. Transport mode protects upper-layer payload; tunnel mode encapsulates an inner IP packet inside an outer header. A VPN is a logical private connection; its actual security depends on the chosen authenticated tunnel.
SSH expands to Secure Shell and provides secure remote login and related network services.
AAA names authentication, authorization and accounting functions, rather than a particular remote-shell channel.

questions.stem: What is a Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) attack?
questions.hint: Identify the trust claim or communication mapping being abused.

answer.text: A man-in-the-middle attack places an attacker between communicating parties to intercept and potentially alter their exchange. Authentication of the intended peer and a protected channel are needed; encryption without authentic key binding can still allow intermediary substitution.
answer.explanation: SEC05 gives the interception/alteration mechanism, while SEC18’s unauthenticated Diffie–Hellman example explains why secrecy mechanisms alone are insufficient. The attacker may relay messages so both victims believe they communicate directly, making peer authentication and correct certificate/key checks essential.

evidence.quote: Masquerade claims another identity. ARP spoofing poisons local IPv4-to-MAC associations; DNS spoofing/cache poisoning supplies false name resolutions; IP spoofing falsifies a source address. An intermediary attack intercepts and can alter exchanges. A replay reuses a valid old message; nonces, timestamps and sequence checks can reject it. Session hijacking steals or predicts a valid session token. Protect transport, regenerate session IDs after login, restrict cookies and check authorization server-side on every sensitive request.
Diffie–Hellman agrees on a secret but unauthenticated DH permits intermediary substitution.
Hybrid systems establish or encapsulate a symmetric secret with public-key mechanisms, then protect bulk data symmetrically.

questions.stem: What is the SET (Secure Electronic Transaction) protocol and who developed it?
questions.hint: Match the communication task to the protocol and trace key handling separately from signing.

answer.text: SET means Secure Electronic Transaction. It was a Visa/Mastercard-led specification for protecting payment-card transactions with certificates and signatures. It is distinct from an ordinary HTTPS connection or a general payment-processing system.
answer.explanation: SEC22 supplies the expansion, origin and protection role. Certificates/signatures support authenticated transaction relationships rather than defining the entire financial settlement infrastructure. Calling every TLS-protected checkout SET would conflate separate protocols with different scope and structure.

evidence.quote: PGP/OpenPGP combines symmetric content protection with public-key key handling and signatures. S/MIME uses certificates for signed and/or enveloped MIME content. Signatures can be sent separately/clear-signed without confidentiality; enveloped data encrypts content and wraps content keys for recipients. SET, Secure Electronic Transaction, was a Visa/Mastercard-led specification for protecting card transactions using certificates and signatures; it is distinct from a payment-processing system or ordinary HTTPS.
TLS succeeds obsolete SSL and supplies an authenticated protected channel.
HTTPS is HTTP over TLS.

questions.stem: What is Session Hijacking?
questions.hint: Identify the trust claim or communication mapping being abused.

answer.text: Session hijacking is taking over an existing authenticated session by stealing or predicting a valid session token. Defenses include protected transport, regenerating IDs after login, restrictive cookie handling and server-side authorization on sensitive requests.
answer.explanation: SEC05 identifies token possession/prediction as the takeover path. Establishing a secure initial login does not alone protect the later bearer token, and checking authorization on every sensitive action remains necessary. The mechanism differs from replaying an old message, although stolen session material can enable reused requests.

evidence.quote: Masquerade claims another identity. ARP spoofing poisons local IPv4-to-MAC associations; DNS spoofing/cache poisoning supplies false name resolutions; IP spoofing falsifies a source address. An intermediary attack intercepts and can alter exchanges. A replay reuses a valid old message; nonces, timestamps and sequence checks can reject it. questions.stem: What is a firewall and what are its three characteristics as a 'reference monitor'?
questions.hint: Separate security-policy enforcement and assurance from ordinary OS features.

answer.text: A firewall enforces traffic policy on flows it mediates. As a reference-monitor design, enforcement must cover every relevant access, resist tampering and be small/simple enough to analyze. For a firewall this is its traffic boundary, not every host-memory operation.
answer.explanation: SEC28 defines the three reference-monitor requirements and explicitly limits a firewall to traversing traffic. SEC23 describes policy enforcement and bypass limits. Thus complete mediation requires preventing alternate paths within the claimed boundary; deploying a firewall does not make it a universal host security kernel.

evidence.quote: A reference monitor is an abstract access-checking mechanism: it must mediate every relevant access, resist tampering and be sufficiently small/simple to analyze. A security kernel implements core enforcement. A firewall can mediate its traversing traffic but cannot enforce every host-memory access. Assurance is justified confidence that controls implement the claims; functionality is what controls claim to do. A GUI or multitasking support alone does not establish trust.
A firewall enforces traffic policy.
Bypass paths, insiders, encrypted uninspected content and infected removable media limit firewall protection.

questions.stem: What is the key difference between a Packet-Filtering firewall and a Stateful Inspection firewall?
questions.hint: Identify which traffic is mediated and what information drives the device's decisions.

answer.text: A stateless packet-filtering firewall matches each packet’s header fields such as addresses, protocol and ports. Stateful inspection also tracks permitted connection context, allowing decisions based on whether traffic belongs to an allowed exchange.
answer.explanation: SEC23 distinguishes header matching from connection-aware inspection. Both can filter ports, so the difference is not port-filtering capability alone. State tracking does not imply unlimited application-content understanding or automatic encryption; those are additional, separate functions.

evidence.quote: A firewall enforces traffic policy. Stateless packet filtering matches headers such as source/destination, protocol and ports. Stateful inspection tracks permitted connection context; application proxies terminate and relay application exchanges and can inspect their content. A circuit gateway relays connections, commonly SOCKS, without full application-content interpretation; textbooks associate it with session/transport functions. Such a gateway need not encrypt and is not automatically a VPN.

questions.stem: What is an Application-Level Gateway (proxy firewall)?
questions.hint: Identify which traffic is mediated and what information drives the device's decisions.

answer.text: An application-level gateway/proxy terminates and relays application exchanges on behalf of clients/services and can inspect application content. It differs from a simple header packet filter or circuit relay that lacks full application-content interpretation.
answer.explanation: SEC23 defines the proxy by its application mediation boundary. It can enforce application-specific policy because it participates in the exchanges rather than merely routing packets. That role does not inherently mean encryption or protection against traffic that bypasses the proxy.

evidence.quote: A firewall enforces traffic policy. Stateless packet filtering matches headers such as source/destination, protocol and ports. Stateful inspection tracks permitted connection context; application proxies terminate and relay application exchanges and can inspect their content. A circuit gateway relays connections, commonly SOCKS, without full application-content interpretation; textbooks associate it with session/transport functions. Such a gateway need not encrypt and is not automatically a VPN.

questions.stem: What is the difference between an IDS and an IPS?
questions.hint: Separate observation from blocking and sensor placement from detection method.

answer.text: An IDS detects suspicious activity and alerts. An IPS can enforce prevention/blocking, usually on the traffic path. Both need contextual analysis because false positives and missed attacks remain possible.
answer.explanation: SEC24 makes action the distinction, independently of host/network sensor location or signature/anomaly detection method. Observing a suspected attack does not itself prevent it. Inline blocking can affect legitimate service when an alert is false, so evidence and policy determine the appropriate response.

evidence.quote: An IDS observes and alerts; an IPS can enforce blocking, usually inline. Host-based sensors examine host events, network-based sensors inspect traffic. Signature detection recognizes known patterns; anomaly detection compares with a baseline and may detect novel behavior. Neither guarantees every attack is detected; anomaly detection can raise many false positives, and signatures can sometimes match variants.
A true positive is a real attack detected, false negative is a missed attack, false positive is innocent activity flagged, and true negative is innocent activity accepted.
Obfuscation makes code harder to understand and can hamper analysis, but does not reliably protect embedded secrets or remove vulnerabilities.

questions.stem: What are the two main types of IDS detection methods?
questions.hint: Separate observation from blocking and sensor placement from detection method.

answer.text: The two main detection methods are signature-based and anomaly-based. Signatures recognize known patterns; anomaly methods compare behavior with a baseline and may find novel deviations. Both can miss attacks or produce false positives.

Host-based versus network-based describes sensor placement, a different classification from how the detection decision is made.

questions.stem: What limitation does a firewall have regarding data outside its perimeter?
questions.hint: Identify which traffic is mediated and what information drives the device's decisions.

answer.text: A firewall cannot enforce policy on data or attack paths that bypass it. Insiders, removable media and uninspected encrypted content can evade its protection, so outside/perimeter-bypassing data needs endpoint, access and other controls.
answer.explanation: SEC23 confines firewall protection to traffic actually mediated and inspectable under its design. A boundary rule does not sanitize every file after it arrives through another path. This is a scope limitation rather than proof that firewalls are useless or that all encrypted traffic is malicious.

evidence.quote: Host firewalls protect individual machines; network firewalls segment networks and can create a DMZ for public-facing services. Rules should be explicit, ordered as implemented, least-privilege and logged appropriately. Stateful and next-generation devices can also filter ports; port filtering is not exclusive to one firewall category. Bypass paths, insiders, encrypted uninspected content and infected removable media limit firewall protection. Hardware firewall does not imply any fixed number of ports.

questions.stem: What is PGP (Pretty Good Privacy) and what security services does it provide?
questions.hint: Match the communication task to the protocol and trace key handling separately from signing.

answer.text: PGP (Pretty Good Privacy)/OpenPGP combines symmetric encryption for content, public-key handling of content keys and digital signatures. It can provide confidentiality and integrity/origin-authentication evidence according to which operations are used and how keys are validated.
answer.explanation: SEC22 gives the hybrid composition and SEC20 explains signature scope. A signature alone does not conceal content; encryption alone is not the same as a validated signature. Recipient/signer key authenticity and custody therefore matter to the protection actually obtained.

evidence.quote: PGP/OpenPGP combines symmetric content protection with public-key key handling and signatures. S/MIME uses certificates for signed and/or enveloped MIME content. Signatures can be sent separately/clear-signed without confidentiality; enveloped data encrypts content and wraps content keys for recipients. SET, Secure Electronic Transaction, was a Visa/Mastercard-led specification for protecting card transactions using certificates and signatures; it is distinct from a payment-processing system or ordinary HTTPS.
PGP expands to Pretty Good Privacy; its message-protection design combines conventional and public-key encryption with digital signatures.
Verification checks origin/integrity under key-identity and key-custody assumptions; it does not conceal content.

questions.stem: What is S/MIME and how does 'Signed and Enveloped Data' work?
questions.hint: Match the communication task to the protocol and trace key handling separately from signing.

answer.text: S/MIME protects MIME messages using certificates for signatures and/or enveloped encryption. In sign-then-encrypt, sign the MIME entity, package its content/signature, encrypt it with a fresh symmetric content key and protect that key for each recipient. The recipient recovers the key, decrypts, then verifies with the validated signer certificate.
answer.explanation: SEC22 specifies this construction while allowing other nesting orders with different coverage. Signed data supplies origin/integrity evidence without inherently concealing content; enveloped data encrypts content and wraps keys. Signing is not generic private-key encryption of the whole message, and certificate/key validation is essential to interpreting verification.

questions.stem: In the RSA example where p=3, q=13, and public key e=3, what is the ciphertext for plaintext m=5?
questions.hint: Check key-generation conditions as well as modular arithmetic.

answer.text: The modular exponentiation gives c=5^3 mod(3×13)=125 mod39=8. However φ=(3−1)(13−1)=24 and gcd(3,24)=3, so e=3 has no modular inverse. This is an arithmetic result, not a valid RSA encryption/decryption key pair.
answer.explanation: SEC19 explicitly identifies the defective source example. Showing ciphertext 8 must not endorse the key setup: RSA requires e coprime to φ so a private exponent can invert it. The calculation and the validity check answer different parts of the example, and both must be preserved.

evidence.quote: For textbook RSA choose distinct primes p,q; n=pq and φ=(p-1)(q-1). Choose 1<e<φ with gcd(e,φ)=1, then compute d=e^-1 modφ. Public key is (n,e), private includes d. Encrypt 0≤m<n by c=m^e modn; decrypt by m=c^d modn. Use modular repeated squaring for large exponents. Real RSA requires appropriate standardized padding; raw arithmetic is not a secure deployment recipe.
With p=3,q=13,e=3,m=5, 5^3 mod39=8 arithmetically, but gcd(3,24)=3, so e has no inverse and this is not a valid RSA key.

questions.stem: What is the Hill Cipher and why is it considered strong?
questions.hint: Identify the cipher's unit, key structure and assumptions before judging its strength.

answer.text: Hill is a polygraphic matrix substitution cipher, C=KP mod26. Its key must be invertible modulo 26, with determinant coprime to 26. It is not strong by modern standards: enough independent known plaintext/ciphertext blocks reveal the key through its linear structure.
answer.explanation: SEC14 rejects the supplied claim of known-plaintext resistance. Combining letters into vectors does not remove linear algebraic relationships, and a large-looking matrix key is not proof of modern security. The correct answer explains the construction while correcting the question’s implied blanket strength claim.

evidence.quote: Hill uses C=KP mod26 for letter vectors. K needs an inverse modulo26, equivalently determinant coprime to26. It is linear: enough independent known plaintext/ciphertext blocks reveal K=CP^-1 mod26. Hill is vulnerable to known-plaintext attacks; polygraphic substitution alone is not modern strength.

XSS causes attacker-controlled script to execute in a victim’s browser under the site’s origin.
Stored content persists; reflected content returns in a response; DOM-based XSS can arise from unsafe browser sinks.
Use safe text insertion and context-specific encoding; carefully sanitize allowed HTML.
CSP is added protection, not the sole fix.
CSRF exploits ambient credentials to submit an unwanted authenticated action.
Use unpredictable request tokens and suitable cookie/origin controls.
HttpOnly restricts script access to cookies but does not stop every XSS effect.
Fuzzing sends unexpected inputs to discover faults; it is a testing technique, not itself a category of injection.

A race occurs when correctness depends on timing/interleaving over shared state.
In a check-then-open file operation, another actor may replace the file between the check and use.

Protect the whole invariant with suitable atomic operations, locks or database transactions; locking an unrelated variable does not help.
Vulnerability assessment finds and prioritizes weaknesses; authorized penetration testing attempts to demonstrate consequences.

notes.title: Trusted OS requirements and reference mediation

blocks.text: A trusted OS is relied on to enforce a stated security policy.

Relevant mechanisms include identification/authentication, process and memory isolation, controlled privileges, object access enforcement, protected auditing, safe resource reuse, trusted boot/update paths and recovery behavior.
The trusted computing base comprises components whose failure can violate policy; smaller, analyzable boundaries simplify assurance.
A reference monitor is an abstract access-checking mechanism: it must mediate every relevant access, resist tampering and be sufficiently small/simple to analyze.
A security kernel implements core enforcement.
A firewall can mediate its traversing traffic but cannot enforce every host-memory access.
Assurance is justified confidence that controls implement the claims; functionality is what controls claim to do.
A GUI or multitasking support alone does not establish trust.

Under Common Criteria, define the Target of Evaluation (TOE), its configuration and environment.
A Security Target (ST) states threats, assumptions, objectives, functional requirements and assurance requirements; a Protection Profile describes reusable requirements for a product category.
Evaluators examine developer evidence, test and analyze vulnerabilities against those claims.
A certification body oversees/reviews the evaluation and issues the certification decision; sponsors commission work and developers supply product/evidence.
An Evaluation Assurance Level packages assurance requirements; EAL1–7 express increasing evaluation rigor, not a universal ranking of security functions.
A higher number does not make a product with different scope automatically safer.
CCRA is a mutual-recognition arrangement, not a single worldwide testing laboratory.
A certificate applies to a specified product/configuration and claims, not immunity to all future attacks.

notes.title: Database secrecy, permissions and key boundaries

blocks.text: Database security needs confidentiality, integrity, availability and accountability together.
Authenticate connections, give roles only necessary table/column/row privileges, restrict views and audit sensitive changes.
A user allowed to read a report need not read the underlying full table.
Check application-level authorization as well as database rights.
Encryption at rest protects stolen storage/backups when keys remain separate; transport encryption protects the connection.
Neither prevents a fully authorized query or guarantees correctness.
Strong access controls, encryption and protected transmission can all contribute to secrecy; compare their roles and assumptions.
Replication is useful for availability but also copies malicious updates unless separate recovery controls exist.
Computer Security module
Integrity requires valid data and valid transitions.
NOT NULL rejects missing mandatory values; UNIQUE/primary keys prevent duplicate identifiers; foreign keys preserve references; CHECK enforces declared predicates.
Transactions group a transfer’s debit and credit atomically; concurrency control prevents unsafe interleavings.
Roles/ACLs limit who may update, but constraints and transaction logic determine whether an authorized update is valid.
Write-ahead logging persists recovery records before dependent data-file changes, supporting recovery after a crash.
Backups, restore tests and separately protected logs recover from deletion/corruption; replication provides alternate service capacity but does not replace backups.
Redundancy improves availability only with appropriate failover and independent failure handling.
Distinguish confidentiality controls from reliability controls and from integrity constraints.

Inference reveals protected facts by combining individually permitted outputs with other knowledge.
If a report gives a two-person salary total and one salary is known, subtraction reveals the other.
Blocking direct SELECT of a salary column does not stop that inference.
Restrict small groups and overlapping queries, track query history, coarsen/suppress results, or introduce carefully designed noise; each trades utility against leakage.
A multilevel database stores items at different labels and enforces mandatory policy using subject clearances, classifications and compartments.
Bell–LaPadula-style read/write restrictions prevent direct downward confidentiality flow; trusted declassification is a separate controlled action.
Views alone are not proof of multilevel isolation.
Covert channels, query results and error messages may still reveal information, so evaluate both direct access and indirect inference.

notes.title: Policy, incident response and recovery objectives

blocks.text: A security policy states responsibilities and rules; a procedure supplies the steps.
Policies coordinate protection, reduce risk and define acceptable use, access review, incident handling and recovery.
They do not prescribe merely “passive system use.” Awareness training teaches reporting and independent verification; enforcement and usable procedures make it operational.
Prepare response roles/tools, detect and analyze, contain the incident, eradicate the cause, restore verified service and learn from the evidence.
Preserve useful protected logs.
Disaster recovery restores IT after disruption; business continuity sustains business functions through workarounds and alternate facilities.
RTO is a recovery-time target; RPO measures the tolerable age of lost data.
A backup schedule must satisfy the required recovery point, and a restore test must demonstrate that data can actually be recovered.

notes.title: Interpret security mechanisms and conditions precisely

blocks.text: Compare each security mechanism with the stated requirement and conditions.
Check asymmetric-encryption key directions carefully; signatures do not generically encrypt whole messages with private keys.
Body biometrics do not imply three factors.
SSL and SSH can both describe protected channels; SSH specifically supports remote-shell services.
Read the full option text before matching it to a security mechanism.
Undefined “arbitrary code execution” does not uniquely identify buffer overflow: several mechanisms can produce that consequence.
A database-security requirement can include both availability and confidentiality.
Generic ACLs and RBAC both restrict unauthorized writes but neither independently enforces all integrity constraints.
Evaluation organizations must be identified by the actual national scheme; CCRA is recognition, not an evaluator.

notes.title: Command injection and the data-to-command boundary

blocks.text: OS command injection occurs when an application lets untrusted input affect a command executed by the host operating system, often through unsafe construction of a shell command. The command runs with the application's effective privileges. This is an injection flaw in command interpretation, unlike fuzzing, which supplies varied inputs to discover defects.

Prefer a suitable library API over constructing a shell command. Where command execution is required, keep the executable and arguments under strict control and validate against the expected permitted structure; merely blocking a few suspicious characters is not a general proof of safety.
OWASP — Command Injection

WannaCry, also known as WannaCrypt, is ransomware with worm-like propagation. It encrypts files and demands payment to restore access. Its name identifies malicious software rather than a network-security protocol. Malware names must be distinguished from defensive controls such as intrusion detection, intrusion prevention and physical protection.

notes.title: Distinguish network roles and protocol names

blocks.text: A router forwards IP packets between networks; forwarding alone is different from detecting suspicious behavior or enforcing a firewall's security policy. SNMP means Simple Network Management Protocol and provides a framework for monitoring and controlling managed devices through management information. It is not a remote-shell service.

AAA names authentication, authorization and accounting functions, rather than a particular remote-shell channel. SSH expands to Secure Shell and provides secure remote login and related network services. PGP expands to Pretty Good Privacy; its message-protection design combines conventional and public-key encryption with digital signatures. Protocol purpose matters when several technologies all contribute to security.
